record.original_question: How can one identify a nonlinear system, or at least an appropriate global equivalence class of nonlinear systems, from data at a global scale rather than only along finite trajectories or in local neighborhoods? In particular, how can one detect unstable equilibria and build a theory combining topological methods, topological data analysis, and modern high-dimensional probability, while also clarifying how approaches such as neural networks, Gaussian processes, and Koopman-operator methods can be developed into a global identification framework?

evidence.quote: Nonlinear system identification: Our understanding of statistical finite-trajectory nonlinear system identification is improving, yet it is unclear how to go about identifying a nonlinear system (or equivalence class) globally. In particular, unstable equilibria are hard to identify.
Combining the topological viewpoint with TDA and modern high-dimensional probability theory ... could be a fruitful combination.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a discrete-time dynamical system on a smooth manifold $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ governed by an unknown map $f : M \to M$, observed through finitely many data of the form $(x_i, f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i)$ for $i=1,\dots,N$, where the $x_i$ may be drawn from finite trajectories or from probing points distributed across $M$, and the $\varepsilon_i$ are bounded or sub-Gaussian noise. Two maps $f_1, f_2$ are called globally equivalent if there exists a homeomorphism (resp. diffeomorphism) $h : M \to M$ such that $h \circ f_1 = f_2 \circ h$, so that $f_1$ and $f_2$ share the same global qualitative dynamics, including the location, number, and stability type of all equilibria (in particular unstable equilibria) and the structure of their stable and unstable manifolds.

Develop a statistical learning framework that, from such data, recovers the global equivalence class $[f]$ of $f$ rather than only a local approximation in a neighborhood of a single trajectory. Specifically:

(a) Define a notion of global identifiability and prove conditions on $(M, f)$ and on the sampling distribution under which $[f]$ is identifiable from $N$ samples with high probability as $N \to \infty$.

(b) Provide a procedure that, with high probability, correctly detects all equilibria of $f$ together with their stability type, including unstable equilibria, and give finite-sample guarantees in terms of $N$, the noise level, the dimension of $M$, and topological invariants of the dynamics.

(c) Formulate this procedure within a unified framework that combines topological dynamics (e.g., Conley index, Morse decompositions), topological data analysis (e.g., persistent homology of sublevel sets or of point clouds derived from the data), and tools from modern high-dimensional probability (e.g., concentration inequalities and empirical process theory), and prove its consistency.

(d) Determine to what extent standard nonparametric estimators of $f$ — neural network regressors, Gaussian process regressors, and finite-dimensional approximations of the Koopman operator — can be combined with the framework of (c) to yield such global identification guarantees, and characterize precisely which features of $[f]$ each of these classes of estimators can or cannot recover globally.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in nonlinear system identification, asking for a global (rather than local or finite-trajectory) identification theory blending topological dynamics, TDA, and high-dimensional probability. No published work resolves this program in full; ongoing research on Koopman operator learning, neural network and Gaussian process system identification, and TDA for dynamical systems addresses pieces of it but not the unified global identification of equivalence classes with guaranteed detection of unstable equilibria.

status_evidence.title: Generalizations and Open Problems (zbMATH entry)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists nonlinear system identification at the global scale, with detection of unstable equilibria and combination of topological methods, TDA, and high-dimensional probability, as an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: The question is explicitly listed as an open problem.
